text: Lieb–Robinson bounds (E. H. Lieb and D. W. Robinson, The finite group velocity of quantum spin systems, Comm. Math. Phys. 28, 1972). In a lattice system with local interactions, influence spreads at bounded speed: an operator at distance \(t\) is felt only after time proportional to \(t\). Translation: members are sites, linear relations among their forms are interactions, and degree is time. A non-free element for a new form must be assembled from the members its relation touches, each contributing its onset. Answers. A light-cone bound on the board would say that non-freeness over a form reaches degree \(d\) only through relation chains of length at most \(d/k\). That is the board version of involvement the obstacle needs for private forms. Test. Passed as consistency only: at the pattern level, involvement is exactly such a bound with speed \(1/k\) per member, and the witness \(u^2v^2\) for a relation of length 2 appears in degree \(4=2\cdot2\), twice the onset. No board statement is tested.

trail.text: Lieb–Robinson bounds. Follow-up. Closed: developed into the single-relation light cone of lem:relation-space-tor, and prop:relation-merging-barrier shows that the light cone certifies only a small fraction of the relations beyond capacity.

text: Dynamic programming on tree decompositions (B. Courcelle, The monadic second-order logic of graphs I, Inform. and Comput. 85, 1990; with the treewidth algorithms of H. L. Bodlaender). Problems on graphs of bounded treewidth are solved by combining answers on bags along the decomposition. Translation: members are vertices and relations are hyperedges of the relation hypergraph; chains and stars have treewidth 1. Answers. For relation hypergraphs of bounded treewidth, Tor classes would be glued from the bags' classes, giving local generation. This would cover the chains, which the involvement line could not explain. Test. Passed on the three-member chain: the onset degree and dimension are those of the bags (\(2=1+1\) at degree 5), and above the onset the chain stays below the bag sum. A proof of generation needs the images of the bags' classes, which the run did not compute.

trail.text: Dynamic programming on tree decompositions. Follow-up. Closed: developed into ex:relation-bag-images and thm:coordinate-relation-locality, which show that the triangle, not a tree, is generated by edges, so treewidth is not the governing invariant.

text: The cluster expansion of statistical mechanics (R. Kotecký and D. Preiss, Cluster expansion for abstract polymer models, Comm. Math. Phys. 103, 1986). The logarithm of a partition function is a sum over connected clusters of polymers, dominated by small clusters when their activities are small. Translation: the correction of the board quotient's Hilbert series from the product formula is a sum over connected groups of members and relations, with the degree of a group's first contribution as its weight. Answers. A convergent expansion in which groups of size \(s\) enter only from degree about \(s\) times the involvement onset would give local generation through \(22k\) from groups of bounded size. Test. Passed as consistency on the chain: the leading correction at degree 5 is the sum of the single-relation polymers (\(2=1+1\)), and their overlap enters only at the next degree (\(4=3+3-2\)). This matches the shape of a cluster expansion, whose second-order terms subtract overlaps.

trail.text: The cluster expansion of statistical mechanics. Follow-up. Closed, by this review's own analysis: the degree-zero circuits put a non-local class at the lowest degree, which a convergent cluster expansion with small polymers at low order forbids.

text: Buchberger's criterion (B. Buchberger, 1965; in the syzygy form of D. Eisenbud, Commutative Algebra with a View Toward Algebraic Geometry, Springer GTM 150, 1995, Theorem 15.8, going back to Schreyer): a generating set is a Gröbner basis exactly when a generating set of the syzygies of its leading terms lifts. Answers. Lifting of top syzygies needs checking only on a generating set, so under (a) only the bounded member sets' syzygies and the dependency classes need to lift. The dependency classes are the whole remaining work, which the review's obstacle states. Test. Passed on the circuits: their one non-local class, the dependency, lifts for W's clause shape (prop:degree-zero-circuits), and every other class is local, so the criterion's reduction applies to them completely.

trail.text: Buchberger's criterion. Follow-up. Developed: prop:first-fall-criterion made its reduction exact for W's clause tops (lifting checked on dependency classes only, which are first falls).

Buchberger's criterion. Follow-up. Developed: its reduction test, in the exact form of prop:first-fall-criterion, was run on the tensor dependencies. The combination does not reduce to zero on the weak base, and in the cube model not modulo closed members either (ex:tensor-family-falls).
Buchberger's criterion. Follow-up. Developed: its reduction test, the absorption of the clause sum by closed members, was run on the forced family this cycle, and fails for proper-span members.

Buchberger's criterion. Follow-up. Closed: its reduction test took its exact form in prop:first-fall-criterion and the absorption tests, and the dense-cover statement no longer asks for lifting of individual dependencies.

text: Hamada's formula (N. Hamada, On the p-rank of the incidence matrix of a balanced or partially balanced incomplete block design and its applications to error correcting codes, Hiroshima Math. J. 3, 1973), with the generalized Reed–Muller theorem it refines. It gives the \(p\)-ranks of incidence matrices of points and flats. Answers. The rank of the \(\omega\)'s of a structured family, a spread, a design or a W block, could be computed exactly, which decides its relations. Test. Passed as consistency: the computed ranks of all \(\omega_U\) equal \([t^{2c}](1+t+t^2)^N\) (6, 10, 19, 45), the top-degree part of the Reed–Muller dimensions the formula refines. This adds nothing beyond the Delsarte–Goethals–MacWilliams derivation already in the squared-subspace entry, and it does not address subfamilies of W's shape.

trail.text: Hamada's formula. Follow-up. Developed: the transversality criterion puts the relations among squared spans into point–subspace incidence codes. The local relations of the Desarguesian 2-spread of \(\mathbb F_3^6\) span 37 dimensions, the 3-rank of the line code of \(\mathrm{PG}(2,9)\) that Hamada's formula gives.
Hamada's formula. Follow-up. Continuing: no new work.
Hamada's formula. Follow-up. Closed: its role, ranks of point–subspace incidence codes, served the transversality criterion. The route no longer depends on relations among squared spans.

text: Projective Reed–Muller duality and small-weight codewords of projective-geometry codes (A. B. Sørensen, Projective Reed–Muller codes, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 37, 1991; B. Bagchi and S. P. Inamdar, Projective geometric codes, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 99, 2002). By the transversality criterion, relations with \(A=0\) are point functions orthogonal to all \((N-c)\)-spaces, codewords of the dual of a projective-geometry code, and the tensor relations are duals of projective Reed–Muller codes. Answers. A classification of the small-weight codewords of these duals would list every kind of non-local dependency among few members, local, tensor and any others. Each kind could then be tested for absorption, as alternative (a) needs, instead of locality. Test. Passed: GUAVA gives minimum weights 6 and 18 for the duals of the line codes of \(\mathrm{PG}(2,3)\) and \(\mathrm{PG}(3,3)\) (research/tools/pg_dual_min_weight.g, output research/results/odd-prime-configuration-review/pg_dual_min_weight.txt). These are the weights of \(\mathbf 1_{V}-\mathbf 1_{V'}\) for two \((c+1)\)-spaces meeting in a \(c\)-space, the coverage of a difference of two pencils, as the translation predicts.

trail.text: Projective Reed–Muller duality and small-weight codewords. Follow-up. Continuing: not developed. The certificates found (lem:flat-sum-certificates) are flat sums, the dual objects the lead describes, but no code-theoretic classification was attempted.

Projective Reed–Muller duality and small-weight codewords. Follow-up. Closed: the lead would classify non-local dependencies among few members, so that each kind could be tested for absorption. The tensor and forced families, the kinds found, are absorbed by their own closed members, which are dense. Under conj:dense-cover-generation a dependency needs no classification, only a dense member containing it.

text: Chevalley–Warning and the Ax–Katz theorem (J. Ax, Zeroes of polynomials over finite fields, Amer. J. Math. 86, 1964; N. M. Katz, On a theorem of Ax, Amer. J. Math. 93, 1971). Through the criterion, the tensor relation says that for every \(c\times c\) matrix pencil \(\sum_iw_iM_i\), the number of \(w\in\mathrm{PG}(c,3)\) where it is singular is \(1\) mod 3. That is Chevalley–Warning for its determinant. Answers. Ax–Katz divisibility controls zero counts of forms by their degrees. A description of the signed point sets on which the zero counts of all determinantal forms of degree \(c\) are constant mod 3 would describe all tensor-type dependencies. It would also say whether sparse, W_RS-like families can carry them, which bounds what alternative (b) must handle. Test. Passed: the degree condition predicts no relation for \(m=c\) and exactly one for \(m=c+1\), and both are confirmed for \(c=2,3\) (Part 4 of transversal_relations.txt).

trail.text: Chevalley–Warning and the Ax–Katz theorem. Follow-up. Continuing: no new work.

Chevalley–Warning and the Ax–Katz theorem. Follow-up. Closed: the lead would describe which sparse families carry tensor-type dependencies. By prop:value-space-satisfiability every family within budget is satisfiable on its value space, so any such dependency sits inside the family's own dense closed member. The question left is about the base's image, where zero counts of determinants do not enter.

text: The Combinatorial Nullstellensatz (N. Alon, Combinatorial Nullstellensatz, Combin. Probab. Comput. 8, 1999). A nonzero polynomial of degree \(d\) is nonzero somewhere on a grid \(S_1\times\dots\times S_r\) with \(|S_i|>\) its degree in each variable. Answers. If the base maps onto a grid in the form values, every nonzero clause sum is visible on it. Tensor dependencies then cannot lift for forms in general position on the base, which decides the lifting question and leaves only alternatives (a) and (b). Test. Passed: on the 7-by-6 weak base six random dense forms map onto all of \(\mathbb F_3^6\), and the tensor clause sum is nonzero at about two thirds of the base points (three seeds).

trail.text: The Combinatorial Nullstellensatz. Follow-up. Closed: its role, showing that tensor dependencies cannot lift once the base maps onto the forms' value space, was settled by the weak-base computation of the configuration review. With the route's statement now about satisfiable members, lifting is no longer needed.

text: The nerve theorem and the Čech-to-derived spectral sequence for covers (J. Leray, 1950; see A. Björner, Topological methods, in Handbook of Combinatorics, 1995, Theorem 10.6). A cover's local data generate the global data when the cover's intersections are acyclic. Answers. For the cover by satisfiable closed members, a Leray-type acyclicity of their intersections, whose allowed sets are intersections of allowed sets, would give generation. The obstacle becomes a statement about the nerve of the satisfiable clause sets. Test. Passed as consistency: the cover of the \(c=2\) tensor family by its 13 line sets, where generation fails, has as nerve the complex of lines through common members. That nerve is a union of 13 tetrahedra, one per member, glued at single vertices, so it is homotopy equivalent to the incidence graph of \(\mathrm{PG}(2,3)\): 26 vertices, 52 edges, first Betti number \(52-26+1=27\ne0\). Adding the whole family, a satisfiable member, makes the nerve a cone and generation holds.

trail.text: The nerve theorem for covers. Follow-up. Continuing: for dense covers any two members meet, so the nerve's 1-skeleton is complete, and cor:value-space-dense-covers makes the value-space nerve a full simplex. The base-image nerve was not computed.

The nerve theorem for covers. The coupled pair's cover by its two members has an edge as nerve, contractible, yet the union is not row-free. Follow-up. Closed: the nerve's topology does not see the failure, which lies in the Jordan type along the coupling.

text: Additivity of ideals of unions of point sets, as in the record's stable unions and the Mayer–Vietoris sequence \(0\to I(P\cup Q)\to I(P)\oplus I(Q)\to I(P)+I(Q)\to0\). Answers. Generation by satisfiable members at the first degree is the statement that \(I(\bigcap_bP_b)_{\le d}\) is the sum of the \(I(\bigcap_{b\in S}P_b)_{\le d}\) over satisfiable \(S\). An additivity theorem for intersections of allowed sets, below the fill point, would give it degree by degree. Test. Passed as consistency, on the same evidence as the falsification attempt, with no separate computation: the tensor and forced falls are exactly failures of additivity for the proper-span covers, and additivity holds trivially once the whole satisfiable family is a member.

trail.text: Additivity of ideals of unions. Follow-up. Continuing: no new work beyond the collapse, which is a failure of additivity for non-dense members.

Additivity of ideals of unions. The coupled pair is a failure of additivity for row freeness: two row-free members, with a union that is not row-free. The cylinder restores additivity at a bounded density cost. Follow-up. Continuing: whether a cover generated by cylinder-repaired members is additive beyond pairs is the next cover-route question.

Additivity of ideals of unions. The Pauling test above is its counting shadow: additivity of allowed fractions holds without couplings and fails with them. Follow-up. Continuing: the Kotecký–Preiss lead is its algebraic development for dilute families.
Additivity of ideals of unions. It became end-additivity: single directions add by block ends, several do not. Follow-up. Continuing: statement 1 is its precise form.

Additivity of ideals of unions. The pair level is now settled: pairs add without overlap below \(\delta_b+\delta_c\) (lem:pair-directness-range). Follow-up. Continuing: many-member additivity is the first obstacle.

Additivity of ideals of unions. Pairs are settled (lem:pair-directness-range, prop:overlap-orientation), and many-member additivity is cover generation between halves. Follow-up. Closed: merged into the obstacle.

text: The sunflower lemma for subspaces and its recent sharpening (P. Erdős and R. Rado, Intersection theorems for systems of sets, J. London Math. Soc. 35, 1960; R. Alweiss, S. Lovett, K. Wu and J. Zhang, Improved bounds for the sunflower lemma, Ann. of Math. 194, 2021). A large family of bounded sets contains a sunflower, many members with a common kernel and disjoint petals. Answers. A subspace version would split any large family of clause spans into sunflowers with kernels \(Z\), which are pinnable (prop:pinned-rank-vacuity), plus a remainder. Where the remainder's clause sets are jointly satisfiable, it would supply the satisfiable members the conjecture needs. Test. Passed, as a structural check of the same two families, with no new computation: they are subspace sunflowers in the weak sense, with pairwise intersections exactly \(Z\), and pinning \(Z\) makes them vacuous with probability \(1-n^K3^{\rho-k}\).

trail.text: The sunflower lemma for subspaces. Follow-up. Developed: flat-covering sunflowers, the shape a dense-cover refutation would take, need about \((\frac32)^k\) clauses on the value space, beyond budget (cor:value-space-dense-covers). Within budget, sunflowers matter only through the base's image.

The sunflower lemma for subspaces. Follow-up. Closed: flat-covering sunflowers are out of budget on the value space (cor:value-space-dense-covers), and couplings, the new obstruction, come from row sums, not from sunflowers.

text: Renormalization by integrating out slow modes (K. G. Wilson, Renormalization group and critical phenomena, Phys. Rev. B 4, 1971). Long-range correlations are removed by integrating out the modes shared across the system, which leaves short-range interactions. Translation: shared subspaces \(Z\) are the slow modes, pinning integrates them out, and the remaining clauses interact locally. Answers. An iteration of pinning until no large sunflower is left, a renormalization flow on the family, would reach a family whose dependencies are generated by satisfiable members, as the obstacle asks. Test. Passed on the two obstruction families, by the same pinned-rank arithmetic as above rather than an independent check: one pinning step of \(Z\) ends the flow, since by prop:pinned-rank-vacuity the restricted clauses vanish on \(\mathbb F_3^{\rho}\) with probability at least \(1-n^K3^{\rho-k}\).

trail.text: Renormalization by integrating out shared modes. Follow-up. Closed: iterated pinning beyond capacity removes capacity-many forms per round at a robustness cost each time. That is the per-block removal of the window review, whose linear ceiling the record recorded.

text: Inverse Littlewood–Offord theorems over finite fields (T. Tao and V. Vu, Inverse Littlewood–Offord theorems and the condition number of random discrete matrices, Ann. of Math. 169, 2009; H. H. Nguyen and V. Vu, Optimal inverse Littlewood–Offord theorems, Adv. Math. 226, 2011). A linear form's values on random inputs are nearly uniform unless its coefficients are structured. Answers. A version for the weak base would say that the base's image under a family's forms is nearly uniform, jointly for small sets of forms, unless the forms have structure. Structured forms are pinnable (prop:pinned-rank-vacuity). Nearly uniform images would make dense clause sets dense on the base as in the value space, reducing dense-cover generation to the value-space statements, where cor:value-space-dense-covers rules out collapses. Test. Passed on the 7-by-6 base: single forms and pairs are within 0.009 of uniform, and images of 8 and 9 forms match uniform samples.

trail.text: Inverse Littlewood–Offord theorems. Developed into lem:weak-base-anticoncentration: below the column-spread scale the base's image is nearly uniform, and beyond it uniformity is impossible. This cycle used it for the density of the coupled pair's allowed set. Follow-up. Closed: the obstacle now lies beyond capacity, where the lemma shows that no uniformity statement for the full image can hold.

text: Hakimi's orientation theorem (S. L. Hakimi, On the degrees of the vertices of a directed graph, J. Franklin Inst. 279, 1965). A graph has an orientation with in-degree at most \(c(v)\) at every vertex iff every subgraph has at most \(\sum c(v)\) edges. Target: conj:row-free-subset for families with pairwise couplings. Answers. With \(c(b)\) the number of cylinder directions member \(b\) can absorb, a repair of all pairwise couplings exists iff the local counting condition holds. This replaces the global obstacle by a density count for pairwise couplings. It breaks for couplings that involve three or more members, which are hyperedges. Test. Passed: the star (one member coupled to \(h\) partners) and the triangle (three members pairwise coupled) both satisfy the count with \(c\equiv1\) on the partners. For the triangle the algebra also goes through. Couple members 1 and 2 along \(w_{12},w_{21}\), members 2 and 3 along \(w_{23},w_{32}\), and members 3 and 1 along \(w_{31},w_{13}\), through three distinct rows, with the six directions distinct coordinates. Orient cyclically: member 1 becomes a cylinder along \(w_{12}\), member 2 along \(w_{23}\) and member 3 along \(w_{31}\). Then the value ring is \(T(w_{12},w_{23},w_{31})\otimes N\), with \(N=M_1''\otimes M_2''\otimes M_3''\). The three row directions act as \(\rho_{12}=w_{12}+n_{12}\), \(\rho_{23}=w_{23}+n_{23}\) and \(\rho_{31}=w_{31}+n_{31}\). Here \(n_{12}=w_{21}\) acts on \(M_2''\), \(n_{23}=w_{32}\) on \(M_3''\) and \(n_{31}=w_{13}\) on \(M_1''\); they commute and cube to zero. This is the tensor product, under the primitive coproduct of the three-variable truncated algebra, of its regular module with \(N\), so it is free. The full freeness of the triangle's subset still needs the analogous pullback hypotheses for three members, which are not checked.

trail.text: Hakimi's orientation theorem. Developed into prop:oriented-cylinder-repair and tested against regular coupling graphs above. Follow-up. Closed: within the column-local framework the orientation count is complete. Beyond it the obstacle is the transfer, not orientation.

text: Carlson's rank varieties and the tensor product theorem (J. F. Carlson, The varieties and the cohomology ring of a module, J. Algebra 85, 1983; E. M. Friedlander and J. Pevtsova, \(\Pi\)-supports for modules for finite group schemes, Duke Math. J. 139, 2007). In characteristic 3 the truncated algebra of a coupling space, with the primitive coproduct, is the group algebra of an infinitesimal elementary abelian group scheme. As an algebra it is also the group algebra of an elementary abelian 3-group. Friedlander and Pevtsova's theory covers both. A tensor product is free iff the intersection of the factors' supports is zero. Target: repair of couplings among many members. Answers. The union's value ring is free over the coupling algebra iff the members' rank varieties, pulled back to the coupling space, meet only in zero. A repair is then a choice of subsets that shrinks the members' varieties until they intersect trivially: a geometric form of the hitting condition. It breaks in the graded truncated setting, where Dade's lemma fails without a special-position hypothesis (ex:truncated-dade-special-position). Test. Passed on the coupled pair, where the coupling space is a line: the union is non-free iff both members are non-free along it (ungraded, by the Jordan-block rule \(J_a\otimes J_b\) is non-free for \(a,b\le2\)). A member whose level sets along \(u\) have unequal sizes is non-free along \(u\): freeness forces \(\dim M=3\dim M/uM\), while \(M/uM\) maps onto the graded ring of every level set, so all levels would have equal size. So part (3) of prop:coupled-pair-imbalance and cor:cylinder-repair are the two sides of this criterion.

trail.text: Carlson's rank varieties. No new development: the multi-directional question, freeness over the whole coupling algebra, needs a graded truncated Dade lemma, which the record shows fails in special position. Follow-up. Continuing: the regular coupled family is where its support-intersection form would be tested next.
Carlson's rank varieties. Continued here as the generic Jordan type lead. Follow-up. Closed: pointwise data cannot certify truncated freeness, by the recorded counterexample.

text: Kneser's addition theorem (M. Kneser, Abschätzung der asymptotischen Dichte von Summenmengen, Math. Z. 58, 1953). It gives lower bounds for sumsets \(E+U\) in terms of stabilizers. The cylinder along a subspace \(U\) removes \((E+U)\cap V\). Target: the per-member capacity \(c(b)\) of the first lead. Answers. A bound on \(|E+U|\) sets how many coupling directions a member absorbs within its density budget. With the trivial upper bound \(|E+U|\le3^{\dim U}|E|\) and \(|E|\le2^{h-1}\), the cost stays below a fixed fraction when \(\dim U\le h(1-\log_32)-O(1)\), about \(0.37h\). Kneser's theorem says the bound is nearly attained unless \(E\) is nearly \(U\)-periodic. Test. Passed: for the \(|K_C|=1\) members of prop:coupled-pair-imbalance, \(E\) is a product of \(\{0\}\) and \(\{1,2\}\) coordinates. Along a coordinate in the support of \(\zeta\) the cylinder adds \(2|E|\) points, and along a coordinate outside it adds \(|E|/2\), matching the trivial bound within a factor of 3.

trail.text: Kneser's addition theorem. Used for the capacities \(c(b)\) in prop:oriented-cylinder-repair and in the falsification count above. Follow-up. Closed: the trivial sumset bound suffices for the capacities, and sharper Kneser bounds do not change which families fail.

text: Semisimplification to the Verlinde category (P. Etingof and V. Ostrik, On semisimplification of tensor categories, 2021; D. Benson, P. Etingof and V. Ostrik, New incompressible symmetric tensor categories in positive characteristic, Invent. Math. 234, 2023). This is quantum topology and conformal field theory. Translation: modules over \(\mathbb F_3[\lambda]/(\lambda^3)\) with primitive \(\lambda\) form a symmetric tensor category. It is not \(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathbb Z/3)\), whose generator is grouplike, and the Verlinde category \(\mathrm{Ver}_3\cong\mathrm{sVec}\) is by definition the semisimplification of the latter. Semisimplifying the primitive category kills the free blocks \(J_3\). By the direct computation \(J_2\otimes J_2=J_3\oplus J_1\) and \(J_1\otimes J_2=J_2\) for primitive \(\lambda\) (in the coupled-pairs entry), \(J_1\) and \(J_2\) then have the fusion rules of \(\mathrm{sVec}\): \(J_1\) is even and \(J_2\) odd. So a member's value ring along a coupled direction has an image, its super dimension, and images multiply under tensor products. Answers. A monoidal invariant detects non-repairable couplings among many members: if the product of the members' super dimensions along a coupling is nonzero, the union is not free along it. Repair must make one factor's image vanish. The obstacle's hitting condition becomes a vanishing condition in a tensor category, where products are computable member by member. Test. Passed with a caveat. The super dimension \(\#J_1-\#J_2\) is an integer and is \(\equiv\dim M=|V|\) mod 3 for every \(V\). For symmetric \(V\) (\(V=-V\)), \(|V|=\alpha+2\beta\equiv\alpha-\beta\) mod 3 as well. For \(V=\{y\ne0\}\), \(M=J_2\) has super dimension \(-1=\alpha-\beta\). The two are different invariants: for the symmetric line \(V=\{y:y_1=0\}\) in \(\mathbb F_3^2\), \(M\) is three copies of \(J_1\) along \(w_1\), with super dimension \(3\), while \(\alpha-\beta=3\). They agree there, but in general they need only agree modulo 3. The super dimension is the multiplicative one, and it is what a many-member test would use.

trail.text: Semisimplification to the Verlinde category. Beyond capacity the allowed set's ring is not a tensor product of members' rings, so there is nothing to semisimplify factor by factor. Follow-up. Continuing: within the column-local framework the super dimension is multiplicative, and it could decide the regular coupled family's non-repairable couplings, which is the next test.
Semisimplification to the Verlinde category. The super dimension is a pointwise, ungraded invariant. Follow-up. Closed: like rank varieties, it cannot see truncated failures.

text: The Kotecký–Preiss cluster expansion (R. Kotecký and D. Preiss, Cluster expansion for abstract polymer models, Comm. Math. Phys. 103, 1986). A dilute gas of polymers with small weights has a convergent expansion of its partition function over connected clusters, when \(\sum_{\gamma'\not\sim\gamma}w(\gamma')e^{a(\gamma')}\le a(\gamma)\). Target: the overdetermined transfer. Answers. Read the blocks' excluded pieces as polymers, and a low-degree function on \(P\) supported on the excluded set as a sum over clusters. In the convergent regime the Hilbert function of the ideal of \(Q\) would be the members' sum plus corrections from connected clusters, each small in number. That is the degree-by-degree computation the obstacle asks for. It would break if algebraic interactions, falls, are not controlled by the weights, since dimension is not additive the way measure is. Test. Passed for the numerical condition. Each W_RS block's excluded value density is at most \(\mathbb E|E_b^{\mathrm{ex}}|/3^h\le3^{-t}\), so with \(M=n^K\) blocks and \(t=(K+1)\log_3n+O(\log\log n)\), \(\sum_bw_b\le n^K3^{-t}\), which is at most about \(1/n\) (smaller by the \(3^{-O(\log\log n)}\) factor when that term of \(t\) is positive). With the simplification \(a\equiv1\), the criterion reads \(e\sum_bw_b\le1\) on the complete incompatibility graph, and it holds with room. The algebraic translation is untested.

trail.text: The Kotecký–Preiss cluster expansion. prop:coupling-distributivity showed the coupled pair's dimension-level correction is zero while it is not row-free. Follow-up. Closed: dimension-level expansions reach only the falls half, which is conj:fill-point-falls.

text: Pauling's ice-rule entropy and Lieb's exact solution of square ice (L. Pauling, J. Amer. Chem. Soc. 57, 1935; E. H. Lieb, Phys. Rev. Lett. 18, 1967). This is chemistry and statistical mechanics. Pauling estimated the residual entropy of ice by treating the local ice-rule constraints as independent, multiplying their acceptance probabilities. Lieb's exact solution showed the correction that correlations make. Translation: blocks are local constraints on the board, and \(|Q|/|P|\) is the acceptance probability. Pauling's estimate is the product of the members' allowed fractions, and deviations from it measure correlation between members through the base. Answers. Where Pauling's product is exact up to small corrections, the members' constraints are uncorrelated on the base, which is the counting shadow of the additivity the obstacle needs. Where it fails, a coupling is present. So the product rule is a cheap detector of couplings, usable at any family size. Test. Passed on saved data (research/results/odd-prime-union-relation/). The ratio \(|Q_a|/(\frac49|P_a|)\), with two constraints \(L\ne0\) of value density \(\frac23\), is between 1.0006 and 1.0256 for the uncoupled control, on both boards and all levels. For the coupled pair it ranges from 0.75 to 1.30. The product rule holds exactly where the Hilbert functions balanced and fails where they did not.

trail.text: Pauling's ice counting. Total counts factor for the coupled pair and the control alike (prop:coupling-distributivity), so counts see couplings only level by level. Follow-up. Closed: the obstruction is not visible in total counts, and level-wise counts are the balance test already recorded.

text: The record's conj:graded-dade-margin, in member form (stated in the pencil graded Dade line, proved for two directions by thm:pencil-graded-dade). Target: statement 1. Answers. The member form replaces cells by member rings and the cell support of a combination by \(\sum_{b\in I}(\delta_b-2)\). The margin \(N\ge4t+2F\) becomes a count of the member tensor's size against the acting space. A proof of the member form through \(D\) would settle statement 1 for families satisfying the margin. It would break if member rings with large \(\delta_b\) admit special positions that cells do not. Test. Passed: the margin needed in W's regime holds by counting. The necessary positivity of \(\prod_b\operatorname{HF}(M_b)/(1+t+t^2)^{r}\) through \(D\), with \(r=\dim K'\), is \((1+t+t^2)^{\sum h_b-r}\prod_b(1-\varepsilon_b(t))\), with \(\varepsilon_b\) starting at \(t^{\delta_b}\). Here \(r=\dim K'\) is of order \(Mh\), and \(\sum_bh_b-r\) is the dimension of the forms' span on the board, at most \(\dim G_1=mN-1\) (\(m\) rows, \(N\) columns of the board, not the one-row conjecture's cell count). Beyond capacity the span is close to \(mN\). So in degree \(d\le D\) the first factor contributes about \((mN)^d/d!\), while each \(\varepsilon_b\) enters only from degree \(\delta_b\approx4t=\Theta(\log n)\), with \(M=n^K\) members. This is a heuristic comparison of orders of growth, not a proof of positivity: \((mN)^{\delta}\) exceeds any fixed power of \(n\) times the members' contributions. The recorded counterexample, outside its margin, is consistent.

trail.text: The record's conj:graded-dade-margin, in member form. Developed through conj:unit-loss-dade, its \(\mathbb F_9\) and pencil checks, and prop:ideal-sum-criterion, which turns it into directness and pair generation of the member ideals. Follow-up. Continuing: its margin form is the first obstacle, for spread families only, since repeated members falsify the unmerged form.
conj:graded-dade-margin in member form. In the dense regime it is now cover generation between spanning halves. Follow-up. Continuing: the obstacle above is its precise form.

conj:graded-dade-margin in member form. It was the value side's freeness statement, which the goal does not need in full (shared-factor falls). Follow-up. Closed: the value side does not reach the obstacle.

text: The plethystic program for counting gauge invariants (B. Feng, A. Hanany and Y.-H. He, Counting gauge invariants: the plethystic program, JHEP 03 (2007) 090). This is theoretical physics. The plethystic logarithm of a Hilbert series lists generators minus relations, degree by degree, and a complete intersection shows as a finite plethystic logarithm. Translation: freeness of \(M\) over \(T(K')\) through \(D\) says that the plethystic logarithm of \(\operatorname{HF}(M)\) splits, through \(D\), as that of the free part plus \(r\) copies of that of \(1+t+t^2\). The first discrepancy is the first non-free relation. Answers. It gives a counting diagnostic, degree by degree, of where freeness fails. This is what a margin statement must control, and it can be computed from Hilbert functions alone, which the members supply. Test. Passed on recorded numbers. For the counterexample the free prediction is \(W=(1,8,22,14)\) and the actual quotient is \((1,8,22,15)\), so the Hilbert-function discrepancy appears exactly at degree 3, where freeness fails. The diagnostic sees the failure; whether it can prove freeness remains open.

trail.text: The plethystic program. Its diagnostic reads the first failure from Hilbert functions. prop:ideal-sum-criterion now gives the obstruction itself, a module of relations, degree by degree. Follow-up. Closed: superseded by the ideal-sum criterion; as a dimension-level diagnostic it cannot prove freeness.

text: The Alexander–Hirschowitz theorem with Terracini's lemma (J. Alexander and A. Hirschowitz, Polynomial interpolation in several variables, J. Algebraic Geom. 4 (1995) 201–222). General double points impose independent conditions on forms of every degree, except for an explicit list, proved by the Horace specialization method. Target: the first obstacle. Answers. By duality, directness of \(\sum_bI_b\) in degree \(j\) is surjectivity of \(T(W)_{2w-j}\to\bigoplus_b(T(W)/\operatorname{Ann}I_b)_{2w-j}\): interpolation on schemes supported on the member spans. A Horace-type theorem for \(T(W)\) would give directness for general spans with finitely many exceptions. It would break if the truncation, which kills cubes, removes the degenerations Horace needs. prop:no-horace-balancing already found no balancing on the PHP board itself. Test. Passed as a structural match. For two double points on \(\mathbb P^n\), quadrics fail by exactly one condition. So does the \((2,4,4)\) pair in dual degree 2, by the rank-one part \(A\otimes B\) that neither square covers.

trail.text: The Alexander–Hirschowitz theorem with Terracini's lemma. Not developed this cycle; the decoupling bridge above is its probabilistic counterpart for random forms. Follow-up. Continuing: a Horace argument in \(T(W)\) has not been attempted.
The Alexander–Hirschowitz theorem with Terracini's lemma, the value side's interpolation route. Follow-up. Closed: same reason.

text: The Hochster–Laksov theorem (M. Hochster and D. Laksov, The linear syzygies of generic forms, Comm. Algebra 15 (1987) 227–239). The ideal of general forms of degree \(d\) has the expected dimension in degree \(d+1\). Target: the first obstacle, one degree above the generators. Answers. Directness of the member ideals in degree \(\delta_{\min}+1\) is the member analogue: linear relations among general subspace-supported ideals. Test. Passed on the recorded data for general position. In \((3,3,3)\) (\(\delta=5\)) all four trials are free through 9, past \(\delta+1\). In \((2,4,4)\) (\(\delta=7\)) trials 1 and 2 are free through 9. Trials 3 and 4 fail at \(\delta=7\), where their pointwise bound is also 6, so they are special position. Falsified for repeated members, which fail at \(\delta\) itself (falsification above).

trail.text: The Hochster–Laksov theorem. Its content, directness one degree above the generators for general forms, is a special case of the orbit-weighted moment for random forms. For adversarial families repeated members falsify it (the ideal-sum review). Follow-up. Closed: subsumed for random forms, falsified for adversarial ones.

text: The spread lemma behind the sunflower bounds (R. Alweiss, S. Lovett, K. Wu and J. Zhang, Improved bounds for the sunflower lemma, Ann. of Math. 194 (2021) 795–815). A family in which no small set lies in too many members is spread, and a spread family behaves like a random one for covering questions. Otherwise some kernel set lies in many members, and one iterates on the link of the kernel. Target: the second obstacle. Answers. In subspace form: either some subspace \(Y\) lies in many member spans, and is pinned (cor:pinned-cluster-reduction) or merged, or the spans are spread. Spread spans should behave like general ones, which is where the interpolation statement is needed. Test. Passed on the extreme case. When all members share one span \(U\), the kernel is \(U\), the residual spans are zero, and pinning \(U\), of logarithmic dimension, settles the family. Not tested: a subspace version of the spread lemma and its degree cost; no subspace form was located.

trail.text: The spread lemma. Developed into prop:overlap-orientation, prop:multi-direction-threshold and cor:cluster-flag-reduction: pairs within budget and local relations are settled. The falsification above shows that adversarial overlap graphs exceed the budget. Follow-up. Developed.
The spread lemma. Its pair and cluster results stand. Follow-up. Closed: the obstacle lies in dense pure relations, not in the sharing structure the spread reduction addresses.

text: The decoupling theorem of quantum information (F. Dupuis, M. Berta, J. Wullschleger and R. Renner, One-shot decoupling, Commun. Math. Phys. 328 (2014) 251–284). A random unitary applied to one half of a system decouples it from a reference, once a dimension (min-entropy) condition holds. Translation: the halves become \(A=(\bar J_1)_d\) and \(B=(\bar J_2)_d\) in \(T(W)_d\), and the random unitary becomes a random \(g\in\mathrm{GL}(W,\mathbb F_3)\). Since \(\mathrm{GL}(W)\) acts transitively on each orbit \(O\), the first moment is exact: \(\mathbb E\,|A\cap gB|-1=\sum_O|A\cap O|\,|B\cap O|/|O|\). If the forms are uniformly random, the family's law is \(\mathrm{GL}(W)\)-invariant, so the second half may be taken to be a random translate. Answers. For random forms, directness of the halves in a degree \(d<2\delta_{\min}\) holds with positive probability once this orbit-weighted sum is below 1. What must be bounded is how much of the members' ideals lies on small orbits, the elements of low essential dimension. It does not apply to adversarial forms, whose only randomness is the prefixes. Test. Passed as a consistency check on \((2,4,4)\), with the dimensions of the quadric pair defect : two 9-dimensional ideals in the 21-dimensional degree-10 space. The orbit-free count \(3^{9+9-21}=1/27\) would predict directness, yet the defect is forced. The forced intersection element, dual to the rank-one part \(A\otimes B\), is a rank-2 functional on quadrics, in an orbit far smaller than \(3^{21}\). So the defect is carried by a small orbit, as the criterion requires.

trail.text: The decoupling theorem. Developed into lem:derivative-propagation, whose base statement concerns spans in general position. Follow-up. Closed: it applies to random forms, and A1 needs adversarial ones.

text: Nullstellensatz degree of the induction principle (S. R. Buss and T. Pitassi, Good degree bounds on Nullstellensatz refutations of the induction principle, J. Comput. System Sci. 57 (1998) 162–171). Target: A1, the depth of falls produced by chains of implications. Answers. Chains are the recorded mechanism by which PC outruns the Nullstellensatz, and their depth is logarithmic in the chain length, which a polynomial family keeps at \(O(k)\). Test. Passed, from the paper's title result as recalled, not re-read (see Falsification attempt): chain falls in families of \(n^K\) blocks have depth at most about \(0.58k\), well below the lag.

trail.text: Nullstellensatz degree of the induction principle. Consequences of the clauses alone vanish on the allowed set, so implication chains among clauses are not falls of the row span; the lead's framing fails, as the single-degree entry recorded. Follow-up. Closed: the chain depth does not bear on the lagged lift.

text: Exactness of the Taylor resolution (D. Taylor, Ideals generated by monomials in an R-sequence, PhD thesis, University of Chicago, 1966; I. Peeva, Graded Syzygies, Springer, 2011, Section 26). For monomial ideals the Taylor complex is a free resolution, so every relation among its first-step generators comes from its second step. Target: the absorbable space. Where it breaks: product tops are not monomials, so the complex need not be exact. Answers. The derivatives of the relations coming from the second step of the complex are Taylor, so absorption needs relations outside that step, a failure of exactness there. Proof, with \(\partial=\partial_v\), lifted Frobenius elements and the convention \(K_{bc}=\tau_ce_b-\tau_be_c\): for a commutation \(f_2\otimes F_1-f_1\otimes F_2\) of two Frobenius syzygies \(F_i=f_ie_b\) of one top, the derivative \(f_2(\partial f'_1)e_b-f_1(\partial f'_2)e_b\) is a sum of multiples of \(F_2\) and \(F_1\). For a Frobenius–Koszul relation \(f_b\otimes K_{bc}-\tau_c\otimes F_b\), differentiating \(f'_b\tau'_b=0\) gives \(f_b\partial\tau'_b=-(\partial f'_b)\tau_b\), so the derivative \(f_b(\partial\tau'_ce_b-\partial\tau'_be_c)-\tau_c(\partial f'_b)e_b\) equals \(f_b\partial\tau'_c\,e_b-(\partial f'_b)K_{bc}\), a multiple of \(F_b\) minus a multiple of \(K_{bc}\). For a Koszul triple \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\tau_a\otimes K_{bc}\), the derivative is \(-\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}(\partial\tau'_a)K_{bc}\): both have \(\tau_c\partial\tau'_b-\tau_b\partial\tau'_c\) at \(e_a\), and cyclically. So the absorbable space is spanned by derivatives of the remaining relations, those the second step of the complex does not produce. Test. Passed on the seed-23 pair in the weak sense of consistency: its absorbable space is 0 among 685 relations. Whether all 685 come from the second step was not checked.

trail.text: Exactness of the Taylor resolution. Its test was found not to discriminate (the sparse failure sets entry's notes), and this review carries it as a lead with the sharper requirement of prop:joint-absorption-rank. Follow-up. Continuing, as the third Outside lead above, not run.

Exactness of the Taylor resolution. Developed in the nontrivial relation bound and relation excess entries: only nontrivial relations absorb, the seed-23 pair has none at its degree, and random pairs below the fill point have at most one. Follow-up. Closed: its question is answered, and for random tops the answer removes absorption as a mechanism.

trail.text: Pseudo-calibration restricted to the design's support. Developed in the nontrivial relation bound entry: a multiplier fixed before the prefixes fails with overwhelming probability, and an adapted one is a point design off \(E\) with a low-degree ratio to the base design, for which no construction beyond the product of prefix quadrics exists. Follow-up. Closed: the attempt reduced it to the adapted-design problem of this review's obstacle, which the relative covering criterion now carries.

text:
Efron–Stein decomposition on product spaces (R. O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Cambridge 2014, Chapter 8). A function on a product space splits into orthogonal components indexed by sets of coordinates. Answers. It locates where a correlation can live. \(\omega^{\ell}\) is a product of single-column functions \(\psi_u\), and its component on a set \(S\) of columns has norm \(\prod_{u\in S}\|\psi_u-\mathbb E\psi_u\|\prod_{u
otin S}\varphi_u\), at most \(\prod_{u
otin S}\varphi_u\). The squared norms of these components are \(\prod_{u\in S}(1-\varphi_u^2)\prod_{u
otin S}\varphi_u^2\), the law of the set of active columns when column \(u\) is active with probability \(1-\varphi_u^2\) independently. Splitting \(\mathbb E_B[\omega^{\Lambda}\omega^{\ell}]\) over orders and applying Cauchy–Schwarz on each part gives \(|\mathbb E_B\omega^{\Lambda+\ell}|\le igl(\sum_{|S|\ge N-d}\|(\omega^\Lambda)^{=S}\|^2 igr)^{1/2}+\Pr[	ext{fewer than }N-d	ext{ active columns}]^{1/2}\). For random dense forms each column is active with probability \(1-1/(m+1)\) in expectation, so, heuristically (a first-moment remark, not a concentration proof), the second term is tiny once \(d\) exceeds a few times \(N/m\), and a near-refutation with correlation \(\eta\) must put mass about \(\eta^2\) on components of \(\omega^{\Lambda}\) of order at least \(N-d\). Test. Passed: the localization follows from orthogonality, Parseval for \(\omega^{\ell}\) and the product form above; it gives a concrete quantity, the high-order Efron–Stein mass of \(\omega^{\Lambda}\), to study for \(\Lambda\) of column-degree \(D\).

trail.text: Efron–Stein decomposition. Developed in the junta-residue classes entry: the localization is correct, but row-sum phases carry full top-order mass without any correlation, so the bound is too weak; the residue-class decomposition replaced it. Follow-up. Closed: superseded by the residue-class decomposition, which gives sharper statements.

text: Local designs ( prop:local-design-criterion , named in the record and not followed on this line; in the Sherali–Adams tradition of consistent local distributions). The exact Nullstellensatz dual of the base plus the closed members is a functional \(\mu\) with \(\mu(1)=1\), killing the row terms, and agreeing through degree \(D\) with a measure on each member's allowed set. Answers. It removes the union: with the members taken to be the single blocks, a thin failure set inside \(\bigcup_bE_b\) is no obstruction, since \(\mu\) needs to look like a measure only on each \(P_b=B\setminus E_b\) separately, where one-block pinning works. The remaining condition is compatibility: a common \(\mu\) whose degree-\(D\) moments are representable on every \(P_b\), that is, killing every degree-\(\le D\) function supported inside one block's excluded set. Test. Passed: with single blocks as members, the maximal-member collapse does not apply, since it needs a member that is a maximal satisfiable clause set and single blocks are not maximal once pairs of blocks are jointly satisfiable, as for random prefixes, where each point lies in a given \(E_b\) with probability at most \(3^{-t}\) (prop:sparse-failure-sets (6)), so two excluded sets cover in expectation at most a \(2\cdot3^{-t}\) fraction; a point design on \(\bigcap_bP_b\) is a special case, and a restricted matching design \(\nu_\rho\) is representable on \(P_b\) exactly when its trace on \(E_b\) is orthogonal to the functions of degree \(\le D\) supported in \(E_b\), which holds in particular when its support avoids \(E_b\); nothing recorded rules out a \(\rho\) with this property for all blocks.
